opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The way I picture it, the interface should feel less like a piece of software you operate and more like a collaborator you talk to. Right now, if you're a medicinal chemist or a protein engineer, the workflow is pretty fragmented. You've got a structure prediction tool over here, a docking tool over there, some scoring functions, maybe a generative model, and you're stitching it all together with scripts and a lot of intuition.

What I'd love is for a scientist to come in and say something like, "I want a binder for this epitope on this target. It needs to be stable, ideally not cross-react with this homolog, and I care about manufacturability." Then the system takes that intent and translates it into a design campaign. It proposes candidates, shows you predicted structures, tells you how confident it is and why, and flags the tradeoffs it's making.

A big piece of that is that it has to be interactive and iterative. Scientists don't want a black box that spits out one answer. They want to steer. So you look at a predicted complex and say, "I don't like that this loop is so floppy," or "Keep this interface but change the scaffold," and the model responds to that feedback. Almost like pair programming, but for molecules.

The other thing I think is really important is closing the loop with the lab. The interface shouldn't end at a list of sequences. It should help you decide what to actually test, given your budget, and then when the experimental data comes back, it gets folded in so the next round is smarter. The model learns what works for your specific problem.

So it's natural language for expressing intent, rich 3D visualization for building intuition, honest uncertainty so people know when to trust it, and a tight connection to wet-lab results. If we get that right, I think it really changes who can do molecular design and how fast they can do it.

astra-6.text:
I think the interface should let you describe what you want a molecule to do, without having to specify every detail of its structure. You might say, “I want a protein that binds to this target, avoids these other targets, and is stable under these conditions.” Those are the design constraints, and the system would propose candidates you could explore and refine.

The interesting part is making that iterative. You generate some candidates, test them experimentally, and bring those results back into the next round of design. So I envision something more like a conversation about the properties you care about, connected to that experimental feedback loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interface should let you start with what you want the molecule to do, rather than requiring you to specify exactly what it looks like. You might say, “I want a binder to this protein, at this site, with these properties,” and then the system proposes candidates. You can inspect those, add constraints, and iterate.

The interesting part is closing the loop with experiments. You make a set of designs, test them, and bring those results back into the next round. So I envision something interactive, where you're steering the design process and the model is helping you explore possibilities that would be difficult to work through manually.
